hints: Think about what happens when the acidic $O-H$ proton of an alcohol meets reactive sodium metal, and what gas is always released.
walkthrough:
Spot the acidic proton**
You have propan-1-ol, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$. Even though alcohols are very weak acids, the $O-H$ hydrogen is slightly acidic and reactive metals like sodium can remove it. The rest of the carbon skeleton is untouched.

Write the balanced change**
Sodium replaces the hydroxyl hydrogen to give sodium propoxide and hydrogen gas:
$$2\text{C}_3\text{H}_7\text{OH} + 2\text{Na} \rightarrow 2\text{C}_3\text{H}_7\text{ONa} + \text{H}_2$$

hints: Compare the three $O-H$ groups: one attached to $C=O$, one attached directly to a benzene ring, and one attached to an alkyl chain, and recall which class is most willing to release $H^+$.
walkthrough:
Rank by familiar strength**
Carboxylic acids are distinctly acidic, phenols are very weakly acidic, and aliphatic alcohols are essentially neutral. So the strongest acid is propanoic acid, then phenol, then propan-1-ol is weakest.
Final answer: Decreasing acidity (strongest first): propanoic acid > phenol > propan-1-ol

hints: Focus on what happens after $H^+$ leaves: how stable is the negative ion left on oxygen in each case.
Think about electron pushing or pulling by the alkyl group, the benzene ring, and the $C=O$ group on that negative charge.
walkthrough:
Think stability of the conjugate base**
Acid strength is really about how happy the anion is once $H^+$ has gone. A stable anion means a strong acid. A destabilised anion means a weak acid.

Why propan-1-ol is weakest**
In $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{O}^-$, the alkyl group pushes electrons toward oxygen by the positive inductive effect. That intensifies the negative charge on an already negative oxygen, destabilising it. So the $O-H$ stays strong and $H^+$ is reluctant to leave.

Why phenol and propanoic acid are stronger**
In phenoxide, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}^-$, the lone pair on oxygen can delocalise into the pi system of the ring, spreading the charge and stabilising the ion. In propanoate, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COO}^-$, the negative charge is delocalised equally over two oxygens by the $C=O$, which is even more effective stabilisation. That is why propanoic acid > phenol > propan-1-ol.

Final answer: propan-1-ol is weakest: $O-H$ strengthened by electron donating (+I) alkyl group, propoxide ion destabilised by alkyl pushing electrons onto $O^-$.
phenol is intermediate: phenoxide ion stabilised by delocalisation of $O$ lone pair into benzene ring.
propanoic acid is strongest: propanoate ion stabilised by delocalisation of negative charge over two $O$ atoms via $C=O$ (negative inductive effect of $C=O$ weakens $O-H$). Any two correct explanations for max 2.

hints: Remember methanoic acid, $\text{HCOOH}$, is unique among carboxylic acids because it also contains an aldehyde-like $H-C=O$ unit and can act as a reducing agent.
Recall which two classic oxidising reagents give a silver mirror or a red precipitate with aldehydes but not with other carboxylic acids.
walkthrough:
Use the hidden aldehyde character**
Draw $\text{HCOOH}$ as $\text{H-C(=O)-OH}$. That $H$ attached directly to $C=O$ lets it be oxidised easily to $\text{CO}_2$ and water, just like an aldehyde. Propanoic acid, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$, has no such hydrogen and is not oxidised.

Choose the aldehyde test**
Warm separately with Tollens' reagent, $\text{[Ag(NH}_3\text{)}_2\text{]}^+$, or Fehling's reagent containing $\text{Cu}^{2+}$. Methanoic acid reduces $\text{Ag}^+$ to silver mirror and $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ to red $\text{Cu}_2\text{O}$ precipitate. Propanoic acid shows no reaction with either.

Final answer: Use Tollens' reagent or Fehling's reagent.
Methanoic acid gives silver mirror / grey solid with Tollens' or red / orange precipitate with Fehling's; propanoic acid gives no change.

hints: Recall why direct heating of phenol with a carboxylic acid gives a poor yield of phenyl ester, so a more reactive derivative is needed first.
Identify the reagents that convert $\text{-COOH}$ into the highly reactive $\text{-COCl}$ group.
Think about what conditions allow the acyl chloride to react with phenol to form the ester $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{CO}_2\text{C}_6\text{H}_5$.
walkthrough:
Activate the acid first**
Phenol is a poor nucleophile and direct esterification is reversible with a poor yield. Convert propanoic acid into the much more reactive propanoyl chloride using $\text{PCl}_5$ or $\text{PCl}_3$ with heat or $\text{SOCl}_2$:
$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOH} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COCl}$$

Form the phenyl ester**
Add the freshly made $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COCl}$ to phenol dissolved in aqueous $\text{NaOH}$. The phenoxide ion attacks the acyl chloride rapidly at room temperature to give phenyl propanoate:
$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COCl} + \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH} \rightarrow \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{CO}_2\text{C}_6\text{H}_5 + \text{HCl}$$
The $\text{NaOH}$ neutralises the $\text{HCl}$ formed and generates the stronger nucleophile $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}^-$.

Final answer: Step 1: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOH} + \text{PCl}_5$ (or $\text{PCl}_3$ with heat, or $\text{SOCl}_2$) $\rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COCl} +$ by-products.
Step 2: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COCl} + \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH}$ in $\text{NaOH}$ $\rightarrow \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{CO}_2\text{C}_6\text{H}_5 + \text{HCl}$ (neutralised).

hints: Look at the far left of the spectrum near $\delta$ 11 to 12 and recall which proton environment appears so highly deshielded.
walkthrough:
Spot the giveaway singlet**
The spectrum shows a singlet at $\delta$ about 11.7 with no splitting. Only a carboxylic acid $\text{-COOH}$ proton appears that far downfield. Neither an alcohol nor an aldehyde alkyl pattern fits, so Z must be propanoic acid.
Final answer: Z is propanoic acid

hints: Recall the characteristic $\delta$ range for an $O-H$ proton in an alcohol run in $\text{CDCl}_3$.
Recall the very distinctive $\delta$ range for an aldehydic $\text{-CHO}$ proton and check whether such a peak is present.
walkthrough:
Rule out propan-1-ol**
If Z were propan-1-ol you would expect an additional signal for the hydroxyl proton in the range $\delta$ 0.5 to 6.0. The spectrum shows nothing between $\delta$ 3 and 11 except the acid peak, so the alcohol is absent.

Rule out propanal**
If Z were propanal, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CHO}$, you would expect a highly distinctive aldehyde proton signal at $\delta$ 9.3 to 10.5. No peak appears there, only alkyl multiplets near $\delta$ 1.1 and 2.3 plus the $\delta$ 11.7 singlet, so the aldehyde is absent.

Final answer: Not propan-1-ol because no peak at $\delta$ 0.5 to 6.0 for $\text{OH}$ proton.
Not propanal because no peak at $\delta$ 9.3 to 10.5 for $\text{CHO}$ / aldehyde proton.
